Recent work supports adaptive negative difficulty rather than simply increasing uniform negatives. [AHNS (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28709) adapts hardness during training to mitigate false-positive and false-negative problems, although its evidence concerns collaborative filtering. More directly, [R²NS (WWW 2026)](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) combines uniform warm-up, efficient global candidate retrieval, and progressively harder sampling from a shrinking top-M set. Random selection within that set reduces deterministic hardest-item selection; it does not establish that selected items are true negatives. Neither paper establishes gains for this specific masked BERT4Rec benchmark.

Sampling correction and false-negative mitigation address different problems. [Correcting the LogQ Correction (RecSys 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331) shows that standard correction mishandles the positive item, which is always included rather than sampled; its evidence comes from two-tower retrieval. [NeurIPS 2025 theory](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/42b7c2f6d320d1fe1afa899a6319d6d7-Abstract-Conference.html) also cautions against claiming unbiased softmax estimation from sampled subsets. Thus, subtracting log-q does not automatically solve finite-sample bias or mislabeled negatives.

Exclude known training positives, limit concentration on the highest-scored items, and track the actual proposal probabilities if testing sampling correction; deterministic top-k truncation complicates correction.
